Built against [wamsoft/krkrz_dev](https://github.com/wamsoft/krkrz_dev) V2.6.5

- **3D scenes, glTF models and VRM avatars**: the new `3d` flip type shows a VRM avatar, a glTF model or a scene built in script on a KAG or World layer, with a transparent background (`doc/kagex.txt`, "Optional parameters for 3d"). It's drawn by the krkrthreepp plugin, which every engine in this release has: Windows, Linux, the Steam Linux package, macOS, the web, Android and iOS
- **VRM characters**: a World character can be a VRM avatar, with VRM animations as its poses and motions, faces made of expressions, blinking, and lip-sync that shows a lip track's vowels (`doc/world.txt`, "VRM Characters"). Vee, the sample's own avatar, joins the Animated Character demo, and the layer demo shows a scene built in script, a glTF model and Vee on layers
- **Live2D models on layers**: the `l2d` flip type plays a Live2D model as it was made, on a KAG or World layer, with its own motions, expressions, blinking and lip-sync to a sound (`doc/kagex.txt`, "Optional parameters for l2d"). The Live2D plugin is still built with your own Cubism SDK
- **The Live2D tools in the Windows and Linux zips**: `tools/live2d` (`setup.py` walks you through it) and `tools/assets/make_hiyori.py` sit beside kagex-release, so you can build the Live2D plugin for your game from the zip alone
- kagex-release 0.14.0 downloads the 0.14.0 engines

The sample game with Live2D (`kagex_sample_live2d_<platform>`, added to this release once it's out) holds Live2D's Cubism Core: by installing or playing it you agree not to copy the Cubism Core out of it, distribute it apart from the game, modify it, or reverse engineer, decompile or disassemble it. It uses sample data owned and copyrighted by Live2D Inc.

Everything in this release is listed in [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/krkren/kagex/blob/0.14.0/CHANGELOG.md).

On Windows the engine needs OpenGL ES: a graphics driver that supports it, or ANGLE's `libEGL.dll` and `libGLESv2.dll` next to `krkrz.exe`.

The macOS app and tools aren't signed with an Apple Developer ID, so macOS blocks them the first time: open the app from the context menu (Open), or allow it under System Settings > Privacy & Security; for the tools, `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine kagex-release kagex-lipsync`. The Android APK is signed with a debug key: allow installs from unknown sources, or use `adb install`. The sample's iOS build is for the Simulator; kagex-release signs a game for iPhones and iPads with your own Apple Developer certificate.
